explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count messages enabled in usp_TestProcedure, increasing network chatter and risking client result-set confusion.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF is explicitly configured while transactions are used later in the procedure, allowing runtime errors to leave transactions open or partially applied.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders retrieves unnecessary wide LOB columns (such as Comments and DeliveryInstructions) and couples callers to schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) from Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary, nondeterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT is redundant on Sales.Orders.OrderID because OrderID is already guaranteed unique by PK_Sales_Orders.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders allows dirty reads and can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows.
Applying YEAR() directly to Sales.Orders.OrderDate prevents sargable date range filtering and forces column evaluation per row.
The year literal 2016 is hardcoded directly in the WHERE predicate on Sales.Orders.
Comparing int column Sales.Orders.CustomerID to nvarchar(20) variable @CustomerIdText causes an implicit conversion.
Using (@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) prevents effective index seeking on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID and leads to poor plan reuse.
LIKE N'%urgent%' starts with a wildcard on Sales.Orders.Comments, forcing a full scan.
Using NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices is fragile compared to NOT EXISTS because any NULL produced by a subquery column causes the entire predicate to return zero rows.
Wrapping Sales.Orders.CustomerID in ISNULL() makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents an index seek on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
CustomerID literal 1 is hardcoded in the filter predicate on Sales.Orders.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) in the WHERE clause prevents an index seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
Inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 on Sales.Orders typically forces a broad index or table scan.
CustomerID literal 1 is hardcoded in the inequality predicate on Sales.Orders.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers omits a join predicate, producing a Cartesian product.
SELECT TOP (1) without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary row from the joined tables.
Comma-separated FROM clause joining Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines obscures join logic; use explicit ANSI INNER JOIN syntax.
SELECT TOP (1) without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary matching order.
Correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines per Sales.Orders row forces per-row aggregate evaluation instead of a set-based join.
Correlated EXISTS subquery against Sales.OrderLines evaluates per outer Sales.Orders row instead of expressing a set join.
The expression CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is duplicated in both the SELECT list and ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list ordinal position, which breaks or changes sorting if columns are reordered.
OFFSET ... FETCH orders only by non-unique Sales.Orders.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker such as OrderID, making page boundaries nondeterministic.
UNION adds an unnecessary distinct sort/hash operator between two branches (OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2) that are already mutually exclusive.
OrderID literal 1 is hardcoded in the first UNION branch.
OrderID literal 2 is hardcoded in the second UNION branch.
Counting all matching rows in Sales.OrderLines with COUNT(*) > 0 performs unnecessary work when only row existence is needed.
Assigning @OrderID via SELECT from Sales.Orders without a unique filter or ORDER BY silently overwrites the variable across multiple rows and retains an arbitrary last value.
Table variable @OrderIds lacks column statistics and can cause poor cardinality estimates compared to a temporary table.
SELECT TOP (5) into @OrderIds from Sales.Orders lacks an ORDER BY clause, inserting arbitrary rows.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders implicitly defines the temporary table schema rather than declaring it explicitly with CREATE TABLE.
SELECT TOP (5) into #ImplicitOrders lacks an ORDER BY clause, selecting arbitrary rows from Sales.Orders.
Cursor order_cursor iterates over Sales.Orders row-by-row instead of using a set-based operation.
WHILE loop performs procedural iteration using @Counter instead of set-based SQL processing.
Dynamic SQL string @Sql is constructed by concatenating @CustomerID rather than using parameterized SQL.
EXEC (@Sql) executes dynamic SQL without parameter binding, preventing plan reuse.
Dynamic SQL string @Sql concatenates @OrderID directly into the query text instead of using a parameter placeholder.
sys.sp_executesql is called with @Sql but without parameter definitions or bound values.
Temporary table #Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped before usp_TestProcedure exits.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result set without rethrowing via THROW or signaling failure to the caller.
RAISERROR is used instead of modern THROW for raising an application error.
PRINT outputs buffered diagnostic text that is unsuitable for production logging or structured error handling.
Business identifier CustomerID = 1 is hardcoded directly in the query against Sales.Orders.
Unlabelled date constant '20160101' is embedded directly in the filter on Sales.Orders.OrderDate.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits a deterministic style code, causing interpretation to vary based on session DATEFORMAT/LANGUAGE settings.
Using COALESCE on CustomerID in the JOIN predicate between Sales.Orders and Sales.Invoices inhibits index seeks and degrades join optimization.
SELECT TOP (1) without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary joined row.
Self-joining Sales.Orders to itself on OrderID retrieves no data beyond what is already present in a single scan of Sales.Orders.
SELECT TOP (1) without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary OrderID.
Sorting Sales.Orders by Comments (nvarchar(MAX)) requires sorting a wide LOB column and causes high memory grant overhead.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without any WHERE filter.
Row-level predicate ol.OrderID > 0 is placed in HAVING instead of filtering rows before grouping in WHERE.
ORDER BY OrderCount is redundant on an ungrouped scalar COUNT(*) query that always returns exactly one row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders carries known concurrency, locking, and edge-case bugs in SQL Server; prefer separate UPDATE/INSERT statements.
UPDATE Sales.Orders sets Comments = Comments, generating unnecessary transaction log writes and locks without changing data.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines filters only on non-key column Quantity = -1 rather than a primary or candidate key.
Magic quantity value -1 is hardcoded in the DELETE predicate on Sales.OrderLines.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a SQL Server worker thread synchronously.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is executed outside a BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH block, risking orphaned open transactions on error.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON alters session state and tightly couples code to manual identity value management.
System stored procedure sp_who is invoked without its sys. schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 restricts all subsequent statements in the session to 1 row and is never reset with SET ROWCOUNT 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories omits an explicit target column list, making it fragile to column order or schema changes.
CategoryID literal 99 is hardcoded directly in the VALUES list for #DemoCategories.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers omits an explicit column list.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' uses a leading wildcard on Sales.Customers.CustomerName, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
User-supplied parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into dynamic SQL string @sql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
sp_executesql executes @sql without parameterizing @CustomerName.
sp_executesql is called without the sys. schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers lacks a WHERE clause, overwriting CustomerCategoryID for every row in the table.
CustomerCategoryID literal 1 is hardcoded in the UPDATE on #DemoCustomers.
Filtering outer-joined table Sales.Orders in WHERE (o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01') eliminates NULL-extended rows and implicitly converts the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
Unlabelled date literal '2016-01-01' is hardcoded in the WHERE predicate on Sales.Orders.OrderDate.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN under ANSI_NULLS ON and returns no rows; use IS NULL instead.
Scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list can force row-by-row execution and inhibit parallelism across Sales.Customers.
The CATCH block handles an error from an explicit transaction without checking XACT_STATE() or issuing ROLLBACK TRANSACTION, leaving failed transactions open.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing the exception via THROW or returning an error status.
Hardcoding WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers overrides the query optimizer and makes the query brittle if index definitions change.
Three levels of nested derived tables (t3 -> t2 -> t1) over Sales.Customers impair readability and should be simplified or refactored.
LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard on Sales.Customers.CustomerName, forcing an index scan on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) retrieves all columns indiscriminately instead of listing required columns.
